newsitem.title: PERU: Freed Peruvian hostage recalls long ordeal.
newsitem.headline: Freed Peruvian hostage recalls long ordeal.

text.p: The invitation to the party had said it would last until nine o'clock. Dress formal.

Six nights later, still wearing his crumpled best suit, Carlos Aquino Rodriguez left the elegant Japanese ambassador's residence, where about 20 armed Peruvian guerrillas had held him and hundreds of others.
"The first thing I want to do is take a shower, the water heater is already on," Aquino, 37, told Reuters in a telephone interview hours after his release Sunday night along with 224 other men.
Despite spending over 145 hours cooped up in a cramped room, sleeping on the floor, with no water to wash in and no change of clothes, Aquino sounded bright and cheerful.
"I feel fine, relieved of course," he said.
Aquino, a university economics professor and brother of local Reuters correspondent Marco Aquino, had been thoroughly enjoying the lavish party until it was dramatically interrupted.

"The Japanese ambassador's parties are always very good because some of the most important people in the country are there," he said. "Suddenly, at about 8:20 p.m. there was a tremendous explosion which stood everybody's hair on end and created total panic."

The rebels later told him how they had pulled off their daring attack by dynamiting the wall of a house abutting the rear of the ambassador's property. Aquino disputed earlier speculation that some rebels members had already infiltrated the party dressed as waiters. "That's not the case, they came in shooting in the air and yelling. It was terrifying."

After releasing the women and elderly, the rebels meticulously censored their prisoners and divided them into different groups -- military officers, politicians and government officials, businessmen and diplomats. Aquino was placed with other profesionals.
The 12-foot (4-metre) by 18-foot (6-metre) bedroom that had been his cell for the duration of his elongated stay at the ambassador's home contained 28 people.
"The 28 of us couldn't all sleep in the same room. In reality about 24 of us could sleep -- even then squashed together head to toe."
The men were closely guarded by heavily armed rebels dressed in commando uniforms who communicated with one another constantly by two-way radio.
"There was always one of them at the door. The idea was for us to be permanently watched."

In an effort to persuade the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas to give up their fight, authorities cut off water, electricity and phones to the residence on the second day of their ordeal.
"It was a really tense, difficult situation," Aquino said.
Critical too, were food supplies which, at first, were scarce. "By Thursday morning it was one roll of bread between five of us."
But as hostages were gradually released, and Red Cross food supplies began to get through, the famine turned into feast.
"By the fourth or fifth day it got to the stage that if we had stayed longer many of us would have left overweight because there was too much food," he said.
Apart from during the first few hours when the MRTA guerrillas were fighting off a brief attack from police outside Aquino never felt that the rebels would kill their captives.
"We suffered no physical or mental harm," he said.
Indeed Aquino grew to respect rebel leader Nestor Cerpa -- one of Peru's two most wanted men -- with whom he spoke twice.
"He explained his strategy and what his movement wanted ... My personal opinion is that he is a cultured man, well-read and quite intelligent."
The hostages' lowest ebb came on Saturday night when fuel for the residence's generator ran out, throwing the home into total darkness.

Cut off from the outside world and without the reassuring television coverage which had kept them up-to-date with the latest developments outside, "we didn't know what was going to happen, everyone was scared witless."
Although hopeful of a peaceful solution for the 140 hostages who remained inside, Aquino stressed that the rebels had not merely seized the ambassador's residence as a publicity stunt.
"When we were saying good-bye they said they were ready for any military attack and were not in the least bit afraid."
